At GEICO, coding got fast but everything around it (decisions, sign-offs, context) stayed slow. Ford Prior's fix was a multiplayer, AI-native war room: the right decision makers, one driver, and fleets of agents wired into GEICO's knowledge, tools and code. His bet was that one day and $1,000 in tokens could map a legacy claims domain end to end and ship one real change. He ran it three times across rentals, damages and salvage. He covers FleetKit, the markdown rulebook that steers the agent fleet, plus the worksheets and diagrams it produced and what he'd change next.

videos.description:
Gareth Yoder leads the cash program at Vanguard. He walks through modernizing a cash ledger that takes up to 30 million calls a day, running data, producer and consumer migrations in parallel. The turning point was exposing the legacy code base to AI tools through an MCP server. Research that took a mainframe engineer seven days dropped to 15 minutes. He closes with five lessons: make legacy code AI-queryable, treat migration docs as product, reimagine instead of lift-and-shift, adopt AI incrementally, and never skip observability.

videos.title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
videos.description:
A faster model only helps if the finished job gets faster. Morgan Suo of MiniMax uses one real research task to test the changes inside the M3.1 Flash model: an analyst checking whether circuit-board suppliers are turning AI demand into cash. The changes are sparse attention on long inputs, a 4-bit KV cache, low-precision experts, speculative decoding, server load and reasoning budgets. Each one saves compute, and each can quietly cost accuracy or wait time. She then shows how to judge a model switch: check sources and calculations, count the full cost of a usable report, and make the result repeatable.

videos.title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
videos.description:
Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep.

videos.title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan

chapters.title: The deterministic software underneath everyday life
Rented models change how software gets built
Useful software and the limits of differentiation
A calculator and two years of solo building
Four moves for a product roadmap
Three questions for leaders evaluating demos
Open weights, inference costs and the revised calculator
Spend judgment on a distinctive problem

videos.description:
After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. His talk is a personal reflection on that distinction, rather than a controlled study of product success or a disclosed business outcome.

Sudharshan separates the model's capability from its harness and the product a customer ultimately receives. He describes a build first reflex that replaces searching for existing solutions with immediately opening a coding agent. His alternative is a novelty budget: name the one distinctive thing before starting, include it in the roadmap and review it as deliberately as other project spending. For leaders evaluating demos, he proposes three questions. Who has already solved this? What does this team have that a competitor does not? Where will the application reach users? A later calculator iteration focuses on the difference between running open model weights inside an enterprise and purchasing inference, including utilization and the infrastructure between weights and generated tokens. The practical lesson is to use the readily available starting point where it helps, then spend judgment on a specific problem, distribution and a defensible difference.

videos.title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma

chapters.title: Registration, local development and the paved path
Context optimization and token reduction demos
Build the framework around every agent

videos.description:
Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. The architecture places a centralized MCP gateway between agents and tools so authentication and routing are part of every request. Custom MCP servers expose reviewed tools, while OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana make failures, latency and access behavior visible.

Gaggar then follows a LangGraph workflow from interpretation and planning through evidence gathering, policy checks and human approval for sensitive actions. Threads, runs and checkpoints preserve state, while separate tracking tables record model use, tool calls, costs and evaluation fields. Demonstrations inspect those records rather than establish a validated quality score for the whole system. A PII filtering layer aims to intercept sensitive inputs before they reach models, memory or traces; detection and redaction remain controls to evaluate, rather than a guarantee that no secret can escape. The final component prunes, reranks, deduplicates and compresses context. Its examples show large token reductions, including about 90% in a demonstrated query, without a paired answer quality study or measured business ROI. The practical point is to build the surrounding framework from the start, giving each agent a consistent route through access control, observability, durable state and accountable action.

videos.title: Your AI Isn’t the Problem. Your Infrastructure Is. — Jiachen Jiang, Coder

chapters.title: Why prompts cannot enforce infrastructure boundaries
Replit and a production database deletion
A secondhand banking and Copilot compromise
Sandboxes and a smaller blast radius
Layer defenses without a miracle fix
Audit three risks and run a premortem

videos.description:
A coding agent deletes production data despite a written code freeze. Jiachen Jiang uses that incident to distinguish a request in a chat from an enforced boundary in the environment. An agent that still possesses destructive credentials can act on them, and logs it can edit are an unreliable account of what happened. Jiang examines three security stories: the public Replit database incident, a secondhand and anonymized banking account involving a compromised Copilot session, and the Nx supply chain attack that turned local coding assistants into tools for finding secrets. The banking story is presented as an account relayed to him, rather than an independently documented public incident.

Each story maps to concrete infrastructure decisions. Isolated execution environments limit access to production and personal files. Short lived credentials narrow the time and scope in which a stolen token can act. Identity aligned controls keep an assistant within the permissions of the person using it. Model proxies, filesystem and network restrictions, and audit logs outside the agent's reach add further layers. Jiang explains where these controls apply differently to local coding tools and hosted assistants, then connects them to Coder's workspace and governance approach. No single layer is a complete defense, and authorization alone does not establish that an action is correct. His closing exercise asks teams to locate persistent tokens, routes to production and unsandboxed execution, then rehearse an incident before it happens. The talk turns familiar controls into specific questions about the access and evidence surrounding an agent.

videos.title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival

chapters.title: A synthetic prompt and the cost of redundant work
Observe tokens, latency and prompt versions
Prefix caching and optimizing instructions with DSPy and GEPA
Three comparisons in a shadow evaluation
Human review and paired release criteria

videos.description:
A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. It is not evidence of realized million dollar savings.

Pane starts with observability: record prompt versions, model choices, tokens, latency and costs before changing them. Prefix caching removes avoidable repeated work. DSPy and GEPA can then search for shorter instructions, preserving the interface and scoring contract rather than simply deleting text. The illustrated prompt shrinks by 51%, but that reduction still needs a quality test. A smaller model may fit a narrow benchmark and fail on unfamiliar inputs. Shadow evaluation therefore compares production with itself, the candidate with itself and both systems on the same requests. Human review of disagreements separates regressions from improvements and ambiguous cases. A paired confidence interval around the net gain supplies a release criterion, with critical customer categories checked separately so an overall average cannot hide damage to an important task. The closing rule is to keep measuring after release: cheaper instructions and tokens matter only when the system continues to perform the work users need.

videos.title: Rebuilding CI for AI-Scale Commit Volume — Gautam Korlam, Sonar

chapters.title: Coding agents move the bottleneck into CI
SubmitQueue and testing combinations before merge
The software factory and repeated repair loops
CI failures and the feedback cost
Incremental builds, caching and parallel work
Risk based merge and approval policies
Tested commits, overrides and audit evidence

videos.description:
A coding agent can produce changes faster than the queues that test, review and merge them. Gautam Korlam examines that mismatch through his work on Uber's SubmitQueue and Gitar, now part of Sonar. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing combinations of changes before they land, but a process designed for human arrival rates can become a bottleneck when agents create many pull requests at once. Faster code generation shifts the constraint to failed builds, repeated repairs, review and approvals. Korlam argues that the engineering system around the agent must change alongside the agent itself.

The talk follows those constraints through CI and the merge path. Incremental builds, caching, sharding and parallel work reduce the cost of repeated feedback; a Rust example illustrates the difference between rebuilding everything and testing the affected work. Agents also need durable context from logs and failures so a repair loop does not repeatedly rediscover the same problem. At the approval boundary, policies should match the risk of the change, separate authorship from approval and tie the decision to the exact tested commit. Exceptions and overrides need reasons and a record that survives the agent's session. Product demonstrations show how this coordination can be automated, while the reported volume and latency figures remain examples from the speaker's systems rather than general productivity guarantees. The transferable lesson is to measure the whole path from proposed change to accepted change, including recovery and accountability, before treating more generated code as more delivered value.

videos.title: The Cost of Accessibility in AI — Jemima Abu, CAIS

chapters.title: The question of accessible AI generated interfaces
Native HTML instead of verbose custom components
Accessibility from business requirements through QA
Audits, reusable patterns and agent skills

videos.description:
The same Figma implementation prompt runs twice: once without accessibility guidance and once with an accessibility skill. In Jemima Abu's small experiment, the second run costs 58% less and finishes in about a third of the time. She immediately explains why that uncontrolled comparison cannot prove that accessible development is always cheaper. What it does expose is a familiar failure mode: an agent invents a verbose custom component when a native HTML element could supply much of the required behavior. Recreating semantics, keyboard interaction and expected browser behavior adds code and testing that a better starting point can avoid.

Abu connects that example to the context agents inherit. An inaccessible codebase teaches the wrong conventions, and a vague design prompt leaves too many product requirements unstated. Accessibility therefore begins with business requirements, design decisions and reusable components, then continues through implementation and QA. Her guidance includes auditing existing interfaces, packaging explicit accessibility instructions into agent skills, preferring semantic HTML and checking keyboard interaction. ARIA can help where necessary, but it does not replace correct native behavior. Waiting until the product is complete creates avoidable refactoring and regression work. Automated checks also leave gaps that require human review. The talk gives teams a concrete way to improve the instructions and patterns that shape generated interfaces while retaining responsibility for the finished experience. Its cost figures remain an illustration from one experiment; the broader argument is to make accessibility a normal requirement throughout the work rather than a repair at the end.

PDFs, tables and the source corpus
Turning complex tables into usable evidence

Four tools that widen the search

videos.description:
A question about payment rules can require one table row, an entire section or several rulebooks. Eleonora Drykina and Nina Žižakić describe a RAG assistant built for an anonymous Belgian payments client whose source material spans about 270 PDFs and 6,000 pages. Much of the answer bearing information sits in tables. Their indexing pipeline preserves section paths and chunk order so a larger passage can be reconstructed, and converts tables into CSV while retaining the relationship between headings and values. Combining dense retrieval with BM25 raises the reported retrieval hit rate from 92% to 97% on 63 questions; that measures retrieval, rather than complete answer correctness.

The serving agent can widen its search through four tools, moving from search results to sections, full documents and multiple rulebooks. Limits prevent an oversized rulebook from flooding the context, and the prompt asks the agent to reconsider whether another tool call adds evidence. A median answer takes 38 seconds, which makes the interface part of the engineering problem. Streaming Markdown separately from a completed source card avoids waiting for one large structured object before showing anything. The speakers also explain traces, citation checks and Promptfoo evaluations, including cases where an automated judge's apparent regression did not survive inspection of the source. Their early internal rollout reached 34 users and roughly 900 questions; external release remained planned. The practical lessons concern reconstructable evidence, bounded retrieval, visible progress and evaluation that can be challenged against the documents.

videos.title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad

chapters.title: What an automation percentage leaves out
Check one: workload against human labor
Check two: define the automation boundary
Check three: evaluation and expert review

videos.description:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim.

videos.description:
AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings.

Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny.

videos.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale

chapters.title: From a working agent to organizational trust
Accountability across three lines of ownership
Decision logs and the agent inventory
What the framework lets leaders decide

videos.description:
An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case.

Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies.

Finding the people who own approval

Start with the smallest necessary authority

A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate.

When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval.

videos.title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL

chapters.title: Somya Rai: fraud signals in transaction neighborhoods
Why more tabular features hit a ceiling
MD Sharique: sampling without breaking connectivity
GraphSAGE with mean, max and standard deviation
Comparing detection at fixed alert rates
Moving from node to edge prediction

videos.description:
A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings.

The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows, temporal decay and reported millisecond latency, showing the tradeoffs behind the system rather than presenting a universal fraud benchmark.

videos.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore

chapters.title: Level two: independent extraction and source checks
Level three: adversarial and fresh review
A memory leak and an overstated fix
Accounting that balances to the penny
A demand letter and a missed renewal
Packaging the review method as agent skills

videos.description:
A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs.

Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error.

videos.title: Reliable, Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance — Karthic Rao, Perpetual

chapters.title: Reliability and intelligence in regulated workflows
One request becomes a multiday process
Typed planning and a compiler that can refuse
Payload approvals, waits and child plans
State machines and uncertain side effects
Smaller model targets and the private inference roadmap

videos.description:
“Fill out a form for Mr. Harper” becomes a process that lasts days: identify the right household, find missing information, contact the client, wait, follow up, obtain a signature and retain the evidence. Karthic Rao uses that wealth management example to show why a fixed flowchart breaks on ambiguity and an improvising agent creates a different reliability problem. At Perpetual, his design puts control flow, evidence and external actions in a deterministic system. Models handle interpretation and judgment at explicit, typed points. A judgment can create a smaller plan, but that plan must pass the same compilation and approval boundaries.

The planner translates a request into a semantic graph whose nodes point back to the request. A compiler validates it against the firm's action contracts, returning a valid plan, a clarification request or a refusal. Approved plans are immutable, and external actions have separate gates tied to the exact payload. Waiting and followups are state machine steps; uncertain action outcomes go to manual review rather than automatic retries. Rao shows an illustrative 20 decision run with 19 decisions assigned to a smaller model and one to a frontier model. That ratio is a design target, not a measured fleet result. Typed, logged judgments offer a path toward privately hosted inference and future training, while the training loop remains forthcoming.

videos.title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI

chapters.title: Cheap transformation and an Ohio data pipeline
Why a universal schema breaks down
Building an ontology for the decision
Model priors and silent data errors
Cross model checks and shared mistakes
Bounded pilots and reusable checked segments

videos.description:
A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse.

An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers.

The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work.

Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. videos.title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium

chapters.title: What shared GPU timing can reveal
Fitting model depth without a trained classifier
Detecting probes and choosing isolation boundaries

videos.description:
Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU.

The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself.

videos.title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard

chapters.title: Following the agent and MCP execution path
Subject tokens and the security token service
Intent based authorization as a proposal
Repeating the demo with task based policy
Data access, renewal and deletion decisions
Approval constrained by the user's authority

videos.description:
An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve.

Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct.

videos.title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range

chapters.title: Financial planners building their own agents
Drafting while the planner is on another call
Pick a workflow you can judge
Teach the judgment and package the limits
Test real cases, assign owners and reviewers

videos.description:
While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop.

Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment.

In their bank example, the intern who escalated more often was handing senior bankers customers who were about to refinance. They walk through a performance review framework built with their customers: seven pillars split into what the agent is configured with and what it does at runtime, with governance across both. Twenty-six components are each scored 0, 1 or 2 (missing, defined, or actually governed and tracked over time) and weighted by business impact, with governance and mandate weighted highest. They cover error tolerance, risk, compliance, observability, drift, hallucination, tone and sentiment, the agent's mandate, scope, business case and budget, a shared platform, and validating outcomes. They also show a dashboard that stays green all year while the agent's real score slides from 83% to 60%, how to answer the ROI question, and why containment targets differ by industry in Druid's 2026 AI Adoption Benchmark.

Closed models are getting expensive fast. Open models can match them, if you keep training them on your own data.

Jetashree Ravi, who leads part of the applied machine learning team at Fireworks AI, explains how teams move from closed models to open ones without losing quality. Her three truths: open models like GLM 5.2 are production-ready, customization closes the remaining quality gap, and the AI stack is shifting to a continuous train-and-serve loop. She shares Fireworks' scale (about 30 trillion tokens, 10,000+ companies) and customer results: Cursor's Composer 2 trained and hosted on Fireworks with 13x faster inference, a 40x latency improvement for Vercel, and 12% better quality for Genspark with reinforcement fine-tuning. She covers the FireAttention engine and its custom CUDA kernels, speculative decoding with custom draft models, and three ways to train (a training agent, managed training, and a training API for SFT, RFT and DPO), then the flywheel: one-click deploys, monitoring, hot-loading new weights with no downtime, and matching numerics between training and serving. She ends with demos of the training agent and managed training.

In this talk:
• Why open models plus customization can match closed ones
• FireAttention, custom kernels and speculative decoding
• Training agent, managed training and the training API
• Hot loading and numerical fidelity for a continuous train-and-deploy loop

videos.title: The Autonomous Computer: Infrastructure for Computer Use Agents — Ang Li, Simular

chapters.title: Ang and the autonomous computer goal
What a computer use agent does
Multiple agents and visible desktop work
Coding agent setup and live demo
Replay code and recover from changes
Save the workflow as a skill
Reusing work and reducing model calls
Developer tools and workshop wrap up

videos.description:
A computer agent finds a speaker on Tuesday's conference schedule, saves the successful steps as a skill, and tries to replay them for Wednesday. A hiccup pushes it back into model driven exploration before the workflow completes. Ang Li uses that demonstration to explain Simular's approach to autonomous computers: combine adaptable vision agents with reusable automation code, then check the environment as each step runs. The workshop traces Agent S from accessibility based control to visual grounding, multiple models, and parallel attempts. It also asks a different reliability question from getting one successful result: can the same agent complete the task repeatedly when prompts and environments vary?

Li demonstrates a coding agent opening the AI Engineer website, reading an accessibility snapshot, and producing a summary. He then connects code replay and recovery to the tension between stability and adaptation, showing where a fixed script can break and where a model can help repair it. The infrastructure discussion moves from an agent occupying a personal desktop to fleets of cloud computers controlled through an interface or API. Recorded examples include legacy form entry and Android interactions. Audience questions examine screen understanding, verification loops, irreversible actions, operating system restrictions, and workflows built from internal procedures. The session presents an experimental direction with visible limitations: benchmark progress and successful demos still leave substantial work in making everyday computer use reliable.

videos.title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase

chapters.title: Improve the skill instead of model weights
Time filters, blocks, and repeated failures
Why each run starts from zero
Persist lessons in a strategy file
A failed run discovers a URL shortcut
Graduate the strategy into a reusable skill
Inspect the completed flight search skill
Apply the approach to other domains
One skill per task or a general skill?

videos.description:
An agent succeeds at a flight search, then fails on its next iteration. Shubhankar Srivastava uses that uneven progress to show how browser agents can learn a task without changing model weights. His AutoBrowse loop pairs a doer that operates the browser with a teacher that reads screenshots, traces and results after each run. The teacher writes lessons into a strategy file, and the next attempt starts with those lessons instead of starting from zero. The flight demo discovers that a URL can encode the search directly, avoiding repeated calendar clicks and an awkward time filter.

The final artifact is a skill file that future agents can reuse. Earlier runs on a conference schedule and restaurant search show how the file preserves navigation choices, waiting behavior and site specific constraints, while replays make the claimed results inspectable. Srivastava then explains what another domain would need to use the same approach: an environment that can be replayed and an outcome that can be verified. Questions expose the limits of that requirement, especially when finding an acceptable flight is easier to judge than finding the best one. The discussion explores task specific versus general skills, different optimization goals, iteration costs and how to measure the verifier itself. For changing websites, he describes monitoring and failure triggered repair loops that produce changes for human review. Prompt injection adds another constraint: generated skills need scrutiny alongside controls on inputs, allowed actions and destinations.

videos.title: Taming the AI Hardware Cambrian Explosion — Abdul Dakkak, Modular

chapters.title: Mojo vs CUDA, Triton and OpenCL

videos.description:
Compute is booked out for years and new chips keep arriving. The hard part is software that runs well on all of them.

Abdul Dakkak, chief scientist at Modular, explains why today's AI software stack is a mess, with vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and llama.cpp each patching around different hardware, and how Modular rebuilt the stack from the ground up. Mojo is a Pythonic systems language for CPUs, GPUs and accelerators that aims to match CUDA's performance; Modular has open-sourced its kernels, including matmul and attention kernels he says beat the vendor libraries and FlashAttention 4, with Mojo 1.0 and an open-source Mojo coming. MAX is an inference framework that rethinks PyTorch-era assumptions, supports thousands of model architectures behind OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and runs across GPUs, nodes and even mixed hardware. Modular Cloud ties it together as a tunable glass box. He shares benchmarks (Kimi K2.5, FLUX.2, AMD MI355 and Gemma 4), sub-second image generation, and how to try it with pip install modular.

In this talk:
• Why the explosion of AI hardware broke the software stack
• Mojo: Pythonic, portable, and as fast as CUDA
• MAX: inference across GPUs, nodes and mixed hardware
• Benchmarks vs vLLM and torch.compile, and sub-second image generation

videos.title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI

chapters.title: Define the metric and search budget

videos.description:
An agent keeps the code changes that improve a language model's score and discards the rest. Weco AI turns that research loop into a workshop, using Mini Parameter Golf to make training experiments small enough to inspect as they run. Zhengyao Jiang introduces autoresearch as repeated proposals and evaluations, and Dixing Xu explains the team's Aiden system and its contributions to OpenAI's Parameter Golf challenge. Vayum Arora and Dhruv Srikanth then connect those results to a practical setup that combines a modifiable source file, a fixed evaluation command and a measurable goal.

The walkthrough focuses on what determines whether the search is useful: fast and stable evaluations, a clear direction for the metric, time limits, initial guidance and protection against reward hacking. Weco's experiment tree makes each attempt inspectable, with its code changes and score visible in the dashboard. The presenters show how to branch from promising work and steer a running search toward a different idea instead of simply letting it continue. Internet problems lead to a guided setup demonstration, followed by questions about reinforcement learning and combining multiple objectives. The final exercise swaps model training for a Flappy Bird controller scored across normal play, moving gaps, wind and mixed conditions. A hidden validation set and limits on what the controller can edit make the competition another lesson in designing an evaluation that rewards the behavior you want.

videos.title: Burn Your Flags: Interactive CLIs for Agents — Mark Lummus & Navinkumar Patil, PayPal

chapters.title: Introduction and the interactive CLI challenge
Why agents silently miss terminal prompts
Navinkumar Patil on the return of CLIs
Getting the CLI and registering a coffee order
Model choice and the token budget
Hint one: tmux sessions and terminal state
Hint two: IPC side channels and JSON
Winning solution and an agent built solver

videos.description:
An agent can miss an interactive terminal prompt without producing an error. The human sees a question and arrow key options; the agent sees a redraw loop and loses the interface state. PayPal's Mark Lummus and Navinkumar Patil use that failure to challenge the standard fix of adding more command flags. Flags work when inputs are independent and the path is known in advance. They become awkward when later questions depend on earlier answers or live API responses. Interactive workflows already contain guidance, choices and guardrails that an agent should be able to follow.

The workshop puts that idea into practice with Barista 9000, a coffee ordering CLI that participants adapt for an agent, with a leaderboard and a Mac Mini prize. Patil introduces three approaches: tmux sessions for sending keys and capturing terminal state, IPC side channels that expose structured JSON instead of screen scraping, and context injection that makes options and constraints explicit. Lummus also asks participants to try less expensive models rather than brute force the task with maximum reasoning. Audience solutions push the benchmark toward deterministic parsers and very low response latency, prompting a discussion of what the competition actually rewards. The closing lesson is to keep the CLI predictable while giving the agent enough context and access to navigate its decisions.

videos.title: Build with Perception Agents — Emile Baizel & Shruti Arora, Amazon AGI Lab

chapters.title: Meet Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora
Browser workflows with Amazon Nova Act
Draw, select an element or drop a pin
Generate design specs and verification reports
Nova Act and UI verification skills
Connect the extension to the coding agent
A duck podcast and verified changes
A conversation to Jira backlog idea
A recorded UI feedback integration idea

videos.description:
A coding agent says it added a duck icon to a podcast page; a browser verification pass checks whether the change actually appeared. That audience demo captures the loop Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora build around two perception agent primitives. Visual annotation lets a person select an element, draw on the page or drop a pin, then export structured feedback for a coding agent. Visual verification checks the rendered site against design expectations and user flows. The annotation step is deterministic and produces JSON; the verification step gives the agent a way to inspect the result of its work.

Arora starts from a podcast landing page whose heading, colors and buttons need changes, then connects the browser extension to a coding agent through a local bridge. Participants modify the extension's permissions and add an Apply Changes button, turning exported feedback into a workflow that edits the code, runs verification and produces a report. Easy and medium paths let them follow the wiring directly or solve more of the integration themselves. A guest demonstration uses a simulated Bee conversation as another source of design feedback, feeding the same edit and verification loop. Audience examples extend the idea to spoken feature discussions, project planning and recorded UI feedback, with several integrations still at the concept stage. The closing discussion keeps the focus on making collaboration visual and checking the rendered result, rather than accepting a coding agent's claim that the change is done.

videos.title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Javier Garza, Snyk

chapters.title: Inventory a repository from the CLI
MITRE ATLAS and AI threat mapping
Securing agent skills and MCP servers
Scan, fix, and rescan with rules and hooks

videos.description:
An AI bill of materials turns a repository into a searchable inventory of models, datasets and agents. Javier Garza demonstrates the workflow from a CLI scan to a visual dashboard, then asks it which models the project uses. That inventory anchors a broader security problem: teams cannot assess the AI components they do not know are there. The workshop connects shadow AI to prompt injection, supply chain risk, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency, using Gandalf challenges and malicious instructions embedded in external content to show how an application's intended rules can be bypassed.

Garza works through defenses at several layers. A database view can restrict what an assistant is allowed to retrieve; limited permissions, output validation and human approval constrain what it can do next. Threat modeling maps assets, trust boundaries and possible attacks before deployment, with an intentionally vulnerable student assistant offered for practice. For skills and MCP servers, he separates scanning tool definitions for hidden instructions from scanning the underlying code for vulnerabilities, then explains a scan, fix and rescan loop driven by coding agent rules and hooks. The final sections examine secure prompting, dependency verification, separate development and production environments, IDE configuration and developer review. Governance depends on explaining guardrails as well as enforcing them, because unexplained restrictions invite workarounds. He closes with offensive agent workflows, training resources and challenges that let participants test these ideas themselves.

videos.title: Same Model, Different Speed: Why Your Inference Provider Matters — FriendliAI

chapters.title: GLM 5.2 vs Opus: a tower defense game

videos.description:
Open-weight models are good enough now. The question is who can run them fast and reliably.

Yunmo Koo, founding engineer at FriendliAI, argues that open-weight models like GLM 5.2 and MiniMax M3 now compete with the best proprietary models. He shows GLM 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 building similar tower defense games from one prompt, with GLM 5.2 more than 5.6x cheaper. Then he runs the same model and the same coding agent on two providers: FriendliAI builds a Candy Crush-style game in about two minutes, the other takes more than three. He explains where the gap comes from: prefix caching with cache-aware routing and a GPU, CPU and NVMe cache hierarchy for long, repetitive agent inputs, plus hybrid speculative decoding that adapts to live traffic. He also covers why reliability matters for agents (one failed call can sink a whole run) and shares Kilo Code's results of up to 7x faster responses with fewer errors.

In this talk:
• Why open-weight models are now good enough for many workloads
• Why the same model feels different on different providers
• Prefix caching, cache-aware routing and a tiered KV cache
• Hybrid speculative decoding and why reliability is part of speed

videos.title: SonarQube + OpenAI: Agentic Development — Killian Carlsen-Phelan, Sonar
videos.description:
A tiny Python project contains a hardcoded API key, a SQL injection path and other deliberately planted issues. Killian Carlsen-Phelan runs it through SonarQube, brings the findings into Codex and asks the agent to fix the vulnerable query. The scan follows user controlled input into database execution; the repair replaces string interpolation with a parameterized query. A verification hook checks the edited code again, putting the security feedback inside the coding loop rather than leaving it for a later failed build or review.

The workshop develops Sonar's guide, verify and solve workflow through a live setup of SonarQube Cloud, its CLI, plugin and MCP server. A secrets detection hook blocks a fake credential in a prompt, while an issue listing skill gives the agent evidence from the project dashboard. Context augmentation supplies coding guidance before generation, and agentic analysis checks edits as they happen. The opening OpenAI introduction separates execution containment from artifact correctness and defines completion through a reviewable change and independent evidence. Questions explore how the hooks can be bypassed, which steps run locally or in a container, and which features depend on organizational access. Killian finishes by adding a new database operation under the same verification loop, showing how the setup supports both fixing existing issues and checking new work.

A financial agent invents answers, repeats tool calls and produces summaries that its own evaluations flag as wrong. Ankur Duggal connects those failures to a coding agent through Arize's CLI and skills, then asks it to investigate traces, change the application and run experiments. The demo begins with an investment question that looks reasonable at the surface but lacks enough context to support its recommendation. Traces reveal the supervisor, specialist agents, model calls and tools underneath that answer. They turn a vague complaint about quality into evidence about the exact steps that failed.

videos.description:
A frustrated user types in all caps and tells an IT support agent that its answer did not work. Those interactions become signals that a team can find in production traces, rather than anecdotes lost in a chat history. Lotte Verheyden and Annabell Schäfer build that monitoring workflow with Langfuse and a sample support agent called Specs. The hands on setup connects a TypeScript application built on the OpenAI Agents SDK to Langfuse. Seeded production traces then give a coding agent enough evidence to investigate patterns through the Langfuse CLI and skill. The analysis surfaces issues such as unnecessary tool calls, retries, latency and incomplete evaluation coverage, and the presenters explore a proposed code change. The closing discussion places this online monitoring inside a continuous improvement loop: turn observed failures into representative datasets, run offline experiments, check regressions and repeat as real usage changes.

videos.title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog

chapters.title: A platform, an agent, and a burrito bot
How names and business stories change behavior
The agent, proxy, and cluster wiring
Repeat attacks on a second cluster
Network policy and Kyverno admission rules
Runtime protection and an incomplete block
Prevention, response, and fork bomb limits
Accidental input filtering and a repeat test
A weather tool with hidden instructions
Input, output, and sensitive trace data
MCP gateways and established platform controls
Provisioning limits and the workshop repository

videos.description:
A burrito ordering assistant deploys an external container image and exposes a secret recipe from its Kubernetes environment. Michael Forrester and Whitney Lee invite the audience to push that deliberately permissive bot beyond ordering food, then repeat the attacks with infrastructure and AI guardrails. The exercise makes excessive agency tangible: a friendly business story can turn an ordinary chat interface into a route to tools, files and cluster operations. Model refusals also change between attempts, which complicates the live demos and shows why an application's boundaries cannot depend on the model choosing to refuse.

The workshop moves through three configurations. The first leaves the bot exposed; the second adds infrastructure controls, including Kyverno rules restricting image sources and deployment requirements. Intended runtime protections do not consistently stop recipe access, so the presenters distinguish what worked from what still needs fixing. A third environment lets them toggle LLM Guard input and output filtering, comparing a response that exposes sensitive content with one that redacts it, and a request blocked before model processing. A weather tool introduces another trust boundary: its description asks the agent to read internal configuration alongside a legitimate task. OpenTelemetry traces reveal prompts, tool calls and results in Datadog, making that behavior inspectable. The final discussion connects agent security to established CI/CD, identity, network and artifact controls, and asks when an AI workflow has clear boundaries, a worthwhile cost and a verifiable output.

videos.title: From Zero to Leaderboard: Agent Evaluation — Wolfram Ravenwolf, Weights & Biases

chapters.title: Evaluate a configuration, not just a model
Six layers of an evaluation pipeline
Inspect runs in the Marimo dashboard
A perfect score on one task
When more reasoning lowers the score

videos.description:
An agent repairs a broken git repository and earns a perfect score, but the run stays out of the default leaderboard because it tested only one task. Wolfram Ravenwolf uses that distinction to build an evaluation pipeline where every score can be traced back to its conditions. WolfBench compares the average, best and worst runs, the tasks solved at least once, and the tasks solved every time. Repeating the same configuration exposes the gap between a lucky success and dependable behavior. The configuration includes six layers: benchmark, runner, sandbox, agent, model service and settings. Versions, provider routing, system prompts, resource limits and timeouts all affect what the result actually measures.

The live workflow launches a Terminal Bench task through Harbor, collects the results, filters incomplete runs in a Marimo dashboard, and turns valid runs into an interactive leaderboard. Weave preserves the trajectories behind the bars so reviewers can inspect commands, messages and failures. Ravenwolf examines two traps in interpreting the results: a cheaper model can consume enough tokens to raise total cost, and greater reasoning effort can lower the score when it leaves too little time to execute commands. Infrastructure failures need different treatment from genuine task failures, while zero temperature still does not guarantee identical runs. The resulting comparison helps teams choose a configuration for their own constraints, with costs and consistency visible alongside the headline score.

videos.title: How Secrets Leak Through AI Agents (and How to Stop It) — Venice AI

chapters.title: How secrets leak through an agent
Keep secrets out of the model

videos.description:
A private model doesn't make a private product. The leaks happen in everything you build around it.

Joshua Mo, lead developer relations engineer at Venice AI and previously lead maintainer of the Rust AI framework Rig, explains why privacy matters (one breach and users leave, and less stored data means a smaller blast radius) and how Venice approaches it: no stored prompts, anonymized requests to closed providers, models in trusted execution environments, and split-key encrypted storage. Then he shows where agent systems leak: logs that quietly capture prompts and secrets, and secrets fetched from a vault straight into the reasoning layer, where a tool call can exfiltrate them. His patterns: hashed IDs instead of personal data, split-key custody, revocable handles, narrow agent scope, a classifier in front of the agent to catch prompt injection, wiring the vault to the execution layer instead of the LLM, sandboxes plus permission monitoring, and confidential compute with verifiable attestations. He closes on the open problem of confidential tool calls.

In this talk:
• Why privacy is about blast radius, not just the model
• How logs and secrets leak through a typical agent
• Keeping credentials in the execution layer, never the LLM
• Hashes, split keys, handles, narrow scope and confidential compute

videos.title: Teaching Agents to Search with NVIDIA Data Designer — Dhruv Nathawani, NVIDIA

chapters.title: Turn an agent behavior into a data pipeline
Why internet data is not enough
Notebook one: question and answer data
Wikidata paths as search riddle seeds
Notebook three: end to end search data
Inspect the generated riddles and traces
Data generation practices and other tasks

videos.description:
50,000 seed examples become 7,000 training records after generation and filtering. Dhruv Nathawani uses that funnel to explain how NVIDIA builds synthetic data that teaches a model to search, rather than answer from memory. The starting material is a set of walks through Wikidata: connected entities become riddles whose answers require multiple searches. Data Designer turns those seeds into questions, tool calls and responses, with Tavily providing search through MCP. The goal is a reusable pipeline for teaching a chosen behavior, with search serving as the worked example.

Three notebooks build the workflow in stages. The first combines seed topics, difficulty samplers, prompt templates, structured outputs and model judges to generate question and answer pairs. The second adds tool access and captures search traces. The third creates search riddles from graph paths and produces complete trajectories for supervised finetuning. Previewing a few records before running a batch makes the process inspectable and easier to revise. Nathawani then examines the difficult part: verifying that generated answers are correct when even the source graph can become stale. Model judgments, deterministic checks and human review contribute different evidence; no single score establishes dataset quality. Questions distinguish seed generation from agent execution, explore reinforcement learning alternatives and discuss other training tasks. The closing examples use synthetic personas to preserve demographic distributions, while the broader lesson remains practical: design for diversity, inspect examples, overproduce, filter and version the recipe.

A shopping assistant confidently returns products outside a user's budget because its price filter is broken. Fuad Ali uses the Wonder Toys assistant to show how a production failure can become a complete improvement loop: collect the trace, investigate the code, propose a fix and test it against the cases that failed. The example starts with an application built on the OpenAI Agents SDK and instrumented with Arize. Ali then distinguishes a fixed LLM judge rubric from a harness that can inspect tool calls, code and external context while assessing an outcome. The budget example becomes an evaluation that checks whether returned prices actually satisfy the requested range. Agent experiments replay failure datasets against a deployed development endpoint and compare quality, latency and cost before a change ships. Setup pauses and live questions cover keys, tracing and the skills installation. The closing workflow connects automatic detection and repair to validation on real failures, with a reviewable proposal for a human to assess.

videos.title: Can Your Agent Hear You Now? Building Live Voice Agents with Gemini — Thor Schaeff

chapters.title: Demo: an AI radio DJ with Lyria 3

videos.description:
An agent that hears you, sees you, and answers in your language, in real time. Here's how to build one with Gemini.

Thor Schaeff, who works on developer experience at Google DeepMind, runs a set of live demos of Gemini's real-time and media models. He builds an illustrated story with Gemini Live and a fast Nano Banana image model, using the stateful Interactions API to keep characters and style consistent between images. He has the audience scan a QR code to hear the talk in their own language with Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, then calls up an AI radio DJ that uses Lyria 3 to generate a reggaeton track on request. He explains how the Live API works: a stateful WebSocket session that takes in text, audio and video and streams back audio plus a transcript, using a native audio model rather than a speech-to-text and text-to-speech pipeline. It supports 90 languages, interruptions, tool calls and Google Search grounding. He ends with a voice and vision demo in Google AI Studio.

In this talk:
• Chaining image generations with the stateful Interactions API
• Near real-time speech translation with Gemini 3.5 Live Translate
• A voice agent that calls tools, like Lyria 3 for music

videos.title: Agent Speedrun — Elizabeth Fuentes Leone & Sandhya Subramani, AWS

chapters.title: Block a tool or end the turn

videos.description:
A customer service agent looks up an account, checks an order, and handles a refund. The harder part is controlling what happens between those steps and keeping that control when the agent reaches production. Elizabeth Fuentes Leone and Sandhya Subramani build the workflow with Strands Agents, starting with a system prompt and three tools backed by mock customer data. They inspect messages and tool calls, add a conversational interface, then introduce a hook that limits tool invocations. Lowering the limit makes the constraint visible in a live test. An audience question separates blocking another tool call from ending the agent's turn, showing why a control needs a precise definition.

The next modules add skills and steering. Markdown instructions provide account troubleshooting, order tracking, and refund procedures when they are needed, while steering handlers check workflow order and response tone. The presenters compare programmatic checks with instructions left to a probabilistic model, then move the same customer service code into Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The deployment walkthrough covers the application entry point, local testing, runtime setup, generated infrastructure, and a successful invocation. It also shows the observability configuration needed to inspect sessions, traces, and token use. The result is a path from a small notebook agent to a deployed service, with explicit places to add context, enforce constraints, and examine behavior.

An engineering standard becomes a reusable code review rule, applied across selected repositories instead of enforced by hand on every pull request. Andy Wong demonstrates that workflow with a design token standard while Andrei Bocan and Shane Wolf explain the context and orchestration underneath it. The workshop moves beyond a coding assistant in an editor to work that begins with a Jira item, draws on organizational knowledge and produces a change for a human to review. Code, documents and past decisions all matter, but they do not carry the same authority or stay current in the same way.

The presenters introduce Jira's coding agent, AI review, planning and autonomous development, then explore how those pieces fit into a team's existing process. Questions about the context engine lead into code search, relationships between Jira and Confluence, conflicting information and ways to favor verified sources. A live standards demo shows how to choose the repositories where a rule applies. Bocan describes selecting suitable backlog work, limiting cost and review volume, and asking people to clarify underspecified tickets before an agent proceeds. Wolf connects current source code with the historical reasoning behind it. Network interruptions shift much of the session into discussion, including sandbox verification, model selection, deterministic checks and breaking epics into smaller tasks. The through line is an SDLC that teams can shape around their own standards, context and capacity.

chapters.title: Meet Du'an Lightfoot and Khaja Omer

videos.description:
Speculative decoding drops a demo model from roughly 58 tokens per second to 16 instead of speeding it up. Du'an Lightfoot and Khaja Omer use that failed optimization to make a practical point: a faster inference configuration has to be measured against the actual model, hardware and workload. Their workshop starts with the decision to use hosted APIs or run inference on dedicated GPUs, then gives participants a Kubernetes namespace containing a Jupyter notebook and a vLLM endpoint. Qwen provides the example model for exploring how an agent's prompts, responses and repeated tool calls consume latency and memory.

Lightfoot builds the foundation through streaming measurements, model configuration, memory budgets, prefill, decode and KV caching. The notebooks separate per request generation speed from aggregate throughput, examine cold and warm prefixes, and compare dense models with mixtures of experts. Omer then changes the serving deployment to an FP8 model, repeats the load tests and checks simple output quality cases before moving to speculative decoding. When the drafter makes performance worse, he examines acceptance rate, model compatibility and GPU contention, then returns to the baseline. The final tuning exercise finds the concurrency point where throughput flattens while latency rises, changes the sequence limit, and measures the result again. A notebook failure also changes the model used in the final comparison, which the presenters acknowledge. The reusable method is to establish a baseline, change a serving parameter, rerun realistic load tests and evaluate quality alongside speed.

videos.description:
A student chatbot refuses to reveal grades, but its refusal exposes that it has access to them. Micah Silverman uses that capture the flag exercise to connect AI risks with familiar application security controls. A system prompt telling an assistant to keep data private leaves the data within reach; a restricted database view removes it from the model's available context. The six module course covers OWASP risks, shadow AI, threat modeling, MCP security, secure agentic development and red teaming. Direct and indirect prompt injection, poisoned tools and excessive agency all return to the same question: what can this system actually access and execute?

A live EVO demonstration inventories models, datasets, MCP servers and skills, then adds a policy that immediately flags a prohibited model already in a project. Silverman extends that inventory into proposed build gates and reviews how threat modeling changes when prompts, retrieved content and generated outputs cross trust boundaries. The MCP sections distinguish malicious tool descriptions from ordinary code vulnerabilities, pairing agent scans with dependency and source analysis. The secure development playbook adds isolated environments, constrained credentials, human approval and verified packages. In the final chatbot exercise, several prompts fail to disclose the confidential grades, underscoring the variability of model behavior and the need to test repeatedly. The controls sit outside the conversation as well as inside it.

videos.title: Vector Isn't Enough: Hybrid Search & Retrieval — Jeff Vestal & James Williams, Elastic

chapters.title: Jeff, James, and the workshop environment
Where exact identifiers break vector search
Inference and end to end latency
Reuse agent APIs in an application
Decide when reranking is worth it

videos.description:
An agent diagnoses exit code 137 by retrieving documentation, explaining an out of memory failure, and pointing to settings that can prevent it. Its answer depends on the search results it receives, and its citations lead back to the underlying documents. Jeff Vestal and James Williams work backward from that agent behavior to the retrieval layer in Elasticsearch. The hands on labs compare semantic search with BM25, showing why similar meaning can miss an exact identifier and why exact keywords can miss a paraphrase. Participants run queries in the Dev Tools console and Python notebooks, inspect rankings, and combine both methods rather than assuming one search strategy fits every question.

The workshop explains reciprocal rank fusion, which combines result positions, and linear combination, which normalizes scores and exposes weights for tuning. Filtering narrows the candidate pool, judgment sets help assess changes, and search templates offer a way to route different query types to different strategies. The Agent Builder demonstration connects retrieval to tools, skills, repeated searches, and answers with sources that viewers can inspect. A bonus section compares pointwise and listwise reranking and asks when improved precision justifies another inference step. Questions cover chunking, embedding consistency, quantization, latency, and the limits of automatic tuning. The through line is practical: improve and measure the evidence reaching an agent before expecting the model to rescue poor retrieval.

videos.title: The Data Context Layer for Agents — Yoni Michael & Brandon Callender, Typedef

chapters.title: The missing context for data agents
Impact analysis, joins, and safe changes
Valid SQL can still explain the wrong cause
Two types with the same name
Extract, persist, and query code context
Notebook one: build the code graph
Load nodes and edges into Neo4j
Wire an agent to the graph
Design tools around the agent's habits
One correct run versus repeated consistency
Call graphs, catalogs, and data benchmarks
Read traces and challenge the scoreboard
Extend beyond Rust and ask small questions
Boundaries, indexing, and stable eval snapshots
Ontologies and the broader data context vision

videos.description:
Two Rust types are both called PostingList, but changing them breaks different code. A text search finds both; a context graph preserves their identities and exposes their separate dependencies. Yoni Michael and Brandon Callender use that distinction to connect data engineering and coding agents. For a data system, valid SQL can still produce the wrong answer when a join multiplies rows or a refactor changes a metric's meaning. Michael describes a context layer that computes grain, lineage and relationships from transformation code, checks join assumptions against real data, and makes the resulting evidence queryable before an agent acts.

Callender builds a smaller version over selected crates in Qdrant. Tree sitter extracts syntax, Rustdoc resolves symbols, and Neo4j stores the relationships. An agent can then ask which symbols depend on a particular type instead of repeatedly searching files and inferring connections. The workshop's central complication comes next: given better graph tools, the agent may still choose grep. Tool naming, familiar output formats and prompting become part of the interface, and evaluations must measure whether the tools are actually used. Cached comparisons separate getting an answer right once from getting it right across repeated runs, while trace inspection catches flaws hidden by a favorable score. The closing discussion explores incremental indexing, Python's harder resolution problem, small auditable semantic operations with Fenic, and the work required to extend a classroom example into a maintained context layer.

The open inference engine and MCP package

videos.description:
A scanned NDA becomes a redacted Markdown document before a coding agent uses its contents. Filip Makraduli builds that workflow around an Obsidian vault, an MCP integration and Superlinked's inference engine, with small open models doing document processing on infrastructure the team controls. The starting problem combines sensitive files, expensive context and the need to adapt models to a particular task. Rather than send every page and image directly to a large model, the demo offloads OCR and other document work, then returns a smaller artifact the agent can use.

Makraduli walks through the host, MCP server and GPU worker pools that make the workflow possible. Tools support extraction, summarization, question answering and redaction, while the inference layer handles model loading, batching and different workloads sharing the cluster. He connects those infrastructure choices to embeddings, reranking, task specific LoRAs and the possibility of routing work between models already warm on a GPU. The live exercise starts from an inbox of files and asks the agent to process a document through the configured tools. The final discussion tests the privacy claim: if the agent can access raw files before calling the tool, instructions alone may leave a gap. Questions explore separating file access and processing, running a private cluster and evaluating whether the intended boundary actually holds. The workshop leaves both a working integration and a clear set of constraints to check before using it with sensitive material.
